idiom_name: a component function taking Modifier/child parameters (Laminar) plus signal state; or Scala.js React hooks
implementation_notes: Scala has no single dominant UI framework, so the pattern is assembled from the ecosystem's building blocks. In Laminar a component is a function and its markup half is ordinary parameters: a Modifier[El] is documented as 'a function that you can apply to an element', and the documentation's own example - a TextInput(inputMods: Modifier[Input]*) accepting vararg modifiers 'to let users configure the component's elements without the component needing to whitelist all possible configurations' - is exactly a headless component whose call site supplies structure and styling, while state lives in Airstream signals; the Scala.js React bindings realize the same split as a hook plus typed prop functions. What replaces the classic wrapper class is the function parameter of type Modifier/Node (or a state-carrying case class), so the behaviour owns the transitions and the consumer composes the DOM.
pitfalls: Reading a signal outside a reactive context captures a snapshot: a script-style component calling .now() on every event does not re-render - reactive state must flow through signals/observers.
Children passed as Seq[Modifier] have no automatic keys, so dynamic lists re-render incorrectly without explicit splitting (Laminar documents the missing-keys pitfall).
Laminar's typed wrappers cover the DOM surface only; touching .ref or the raw Scala.js DOM APIs drops the type safety and the escaping guarantees.
